Well, like I was just saying, I really do try to tell myself it could just be a coincidence. I want to believe I'm mistaken, I really do. Because part of my brain—the analytical part, you know, the part that looks at market trends and risk assessments for a living—is constantly trying to tell me that I'm just reading too much into things.

I try so hard to logic my way out of it. I really, really do. I’ll spend hours, I mean literal hours at night, just going over the guest lists or the conference itineraries, trying to prove to myself that these little signals—the panel topics that perfectly mirror my confidential advisory meetings, the specific people who just happen to pull up a chair next to me—are just random statistical anomalies. I try to be the rational professional I’ve always been.

But... I just can't really let it go. Even when I lay out all the reasons why it could just be a mistake, the conviction that they are quietly tracking exactly which clients I meet with just comes rushing right back. It's like this constant hum in the background of my life now. I try to brush it off, but it just feels too precise, you know? The coordination of it all. It's too specific to just be chance. So, I guess, despite my absolute best efforts to prove myself wrong, I really do believe it's actually happening.

Well, I mean... yes and no. I am definitely still working. I’m still going into the office every day, still logging into the terminals, still doing the baseline stuff. I haven't closed up shop or anything. But... if I’m looking at the actual numbers, and I'm a numbers guy, right? The practice itself has definitely gotten smaller. It’s not like a sudden, dramatic collapse, but it’s this slow, frustrating bleed. 

Because, you see, in wealth management, your entire business is built on relationships and momentum. It's all about the touchpoints. And lately, I just... I miss follow-ups. I used to be absolutely religious about them. You meet someone at a charity dinner, you call them Tuesday morning, you send a customized portfolio proposal by Thursday. That was my whole system, it's how I built my book of business. But now, I’ll get back to my desk, and instead of drafting that proposal, I’m spending two hours analyzing the guest list from the dinner, trying to figure out if that prospect was intentionally seated next to me by the people who are tracking my movements. And by the time I snap out of it, or by the time I feel safe enough to reach out, the window to follow up is just gone. 

And I’ve started avoiding things, too. Like the public panels. I used to do a lot of them—speaking at the Chamber of Commerce, doing these local seminars on tax strategies for high-net-worth individuals. It was fantastic for networking. But now, the thought of sitting up on a stage, looking out at a crowd where I know they might be in the audience, coordinating the Q&A topics to mirror my private meetings from the day before... I just can't do it. I can't put myself in that position. So I make up excuses. I tell the organizers I have a scheduling conflict, or I'm traveling for a client. 

So, yeah, I'm having a lot of trouble keeping up the same level of client contact I used to manage. I used to do quarterly lunches with all my top-tier clients, really hands-on, face-to-face stuff. Now, I find myself pushing them to quick phone calls, or just letting my assistant send a generic market update, because I just don't have the mental bandwidth to sit across from a client at a restaurant and pretend I'm not distracted by the seating arrangements or the music playing over the speakers. I only have so much energy, you know? And when so much of it is tied up in monitoring who knows what about my schedule, the actual client care just... slips. So I am functioning, technically, but my practice is definitely taking a hit. It's really hard to watch, honestly, because I worked so hard to build this client base right out of college, and now I just can't seem to hold onto it the same way.

Well, yeah, like I was just saying a minute ago, it’s been going on for about two months now. So, definitely more than a month. And as for it being continuous... I mean, absolutely. Because part of my brain—the analytical part, you know, the part that looks at market trends and risk assessments for a living—is constantly trying to tell me that I'm just reading too much into things. \n\nI mean, I will literally sit in my office downtown, just looking out the window, and I will try to rationalize it all. I'll tell myself, \"Okay, you met with that major collector on Tuesday, and then on Thursday you got an invitation to a private dinner where the seating arrangement deliberately put you right next to their biggest rival.\" And I'll say to myself, \"That's just Cincinnati. That's just how small and interconnected this city's arts and finance circles are.\" \n\nI try so hard to logic my way out of it. I really, really do. I’ll spend hours, I mean literal hours at night, just going over the guest lists or the conference itineraries, trying to prove to myself that these little signals—the panel topics that perfectly mirror my confidential advisory meetings, the specific people who just happen to pull up a chair next to me—are just random statistical anomalies. I try to be the rational professional I’ve always been.\n\nBut... I just can't really let it go. Even when I lay out all the reasons why it could just be a mistake, the conviction that they are quietly tracking exactly which clients I meet with just comes rushing right back. It's like this constant hum in the background of my life now. I try to brush it off, but it just feels too precise, you know? The coordination of it all. It's too specific to just be chance. So, I guess, despite my absolute best efforts to prove myself wrong, I really do believe it's actually happening.\n\nDoctor: Have you been hearing or seeing things that other people do not?\n\nPatient: No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I know what you're asking, like hallucinations or whatever, right? But no, it's not like that at all. I'm not hearing voices whispering to me from the air vents, and I'm not seeing shadows moving in the corners of my office when I'm working late on a quarterly review. My senses are perfectly fine. My hearing is actually quite good, I had it tested a few years ago when I thought I was getting tinnitus from listening to too many financial podcasts on my commute, but it was nothing. And my vision is 20/20, well, with my contacts anyway. \n\nSo, no, I'm not experiencing anything like that. The things I'm talking about, the signals, the seating arrangements, the invitations... those are real, tangible things. They are actual physical emails I receive, actual printed programs at conferences, actual people sitting in actual chairs next to me. Anyone could see them if they were looking at the same things I am. It's just that other people don't have the context to understand what those things mean. They don't know who I met with the day before, so they don't see the connection when a panel topic mirrors that meeting perfectly. \n\nIt's all very grounded in reality, in the actual physical world. It's just the pattern, the coordination behind it all, that's what I'm picking up on. But no, no imaginary voices or visions or anything like that. I'm entirely lucid when it comes to my physical senses, I promise you that. It's just... it's the meaning behind what I'm seeing and hearing that's the issue.\n\nDoctor: How certain are you, from 0 to 100 percent, that these people are actually tracking you?\n\nPatient: Well, if I have to put an exact number on it, from zero to one hundred... I mean, that's a tough thing to quantify, isn't it? Because like I said, I do try to talk myself out of it. I really do. But if I'm being completely honest with myself, and with you, and looking at how much it's affecting my day-to-day life and my ability to just focus on my clients' portfolios without constantly analyzing every single interaction... I'd have to say it's pretty high. \n\nI mean, I came in today specifically because for a while now, I’ve been so convinced that these certain people in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati are quietly tracking which clients I meet with. It's not a passing thought. It's a conviction. And they are sending me these little signals, you know? Through the invitations, the panel topics, even who sits near me at these networking events and charity dinners. \n\nAnd even when I sit there in my office, looking out at the skyline, and I tell myself it could just be a coincidence—because Cincinnati is small, and these circles overlap, and maybe it's just a statistical anomaly—I can’t really let it go. I just can't. The feeling comes right back, stronger than before, because the pattern is just too specific. So, if zero is 'it's definitely all in my head' and one hundred is 'it is absolute, undeniable fact'... I'd probably put myself somewhere around an 85 or a 90. Because despite all my efforts to logic my way out of it, the belief that this is actually happening, that they are actually coordinating this tracking and signaling... it just won't go away. It's just too precise to ignore.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any periods lasting several days or longer when you felt unusually energized or euphoric, needed much less sleep, or were much more active than usual?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't really had anything like that. I mean, sure, there are times when I'm busy at work—especially toward the end of a quarter or during tax season, when I'm reviewing portfolios and trying to make sure all my clients are positioned correctly. During those weeks, I might stay up a bit later, maybe pulling a few long nights here and there to get everything done. I’ll be running on coffee and adrenaline, just trying to keep up with the market shifts and the endless emails. But that’s just the nature of the job, you know? It’s not some kind of unnatural energy or euphoria. It’s just stress and deadlines. \n\nI’ve never had a period where I felt like I just didn’t need sleep at all, or where I felt unusually, I don't know, euphoric or over-the-top energized for days on end. I'm actually pretty protective of my sleep schedule. I try to get my seven or eight hours every night, because if I don't, I get this awful brain fog, and I just can't function properly. When you're managing other people's money, you have to be sharp. You can't be walking into a client meeting running on two hours of sleep and some kind of manic energy. You have to be grounded. \n\nSo, no, I haven't experienced any of those... whatever you'd call them, those high periods. My energy levels are pretty consistent, mostly just tied to how much coffee I've had and whether I actually managed to get to the gym that week. Even with all this stress lately, all this tracking and the signals, it hasn't made me hyperactive or anything. If anything, it's just made me more tired, because I spend so much mental energy trying to figure out what it all means. But no, no periods of feeling unusually energized or needing less sleep. Just my normal, everyday, slightly stressed-out baseline.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any decline in your work performance or ability to function day to day because of these beliefs?\n\nPatient: Well, I mean... yes and no. I am definitely still working. I’m still going into the office every day, still logging into the terminals, still doing the baseline stuff. I haven't closed up shop or anything. But... if I’m looking at the actual numbers, and I'm a numbers guy, right? The practice itself has definitely gotten smaller. It’s not like a sudden, dramatic collapse, but it’s this slow, frustrating bleed. \n\nBecause, you see, in wealth management, your entire business is built on relationships and momentum. It's all about the touchpoints. And lately, I just... I miss follow-ups. I used to be absolutely religious about them. You meet someone at a charity dinner, you call them Tuesday morning, you send a customized portfolio proposal by Thursday. That was my whole system, it's how I built my book of business. But now, I’ll get back to my desk, and instead of drafting that proposal, I’m spending two hours analyzing the guest list from the dinner, trying to figure out if that prospect was intentionally seated next to me by the people who are tracking my movements. And by the time I snap out of it, or by the time I feel safe enough to reach out, the window to follow up is just gone. \n\nAnd I’ve started avoiding things, too. Like the public panels. I used to do a lot of them—speaking at the Chamber of Commerce, doing these local seminars on tax strategies for high-net-worth individuals. It was fantastic for networking. But now, the thought of sitting up on a stage, looking out at a crowd where I know they might be in the audience, coordinating the Q&A topics to mirror my private meetings from the day before... I just can't do it. I can't put myself in that position. So I make up excuses. I tell the organizers I have a scheduling conflict, or I'm traveling for a client. \n\nSo, yeah, I'm having a lot of trouble keeping up the same level of client contact I used to manage. I used to do quarterly lunches with all my top-tier clients, really hands-on, face-to-face stuff. Now, I find myself pushing them to quick phone calls, or just letting my assistant send a generic market update, because I just don't have the mental bandwidth to sit across from a client at a restaurant and pretend I'm not distracted by the seating arrangements or the music playing over the speakers. I only have so much energy, you know? And when so much of it is tied up in monitoring who knows what about my schedule, the actual client care just... slips. So I am functioning, technically, but my practice is definitely taking a hit. It's really hard to watch, honestly, because I worked so hard to build this client base right out of college, and now I just can't seem to hold onto it the same way.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been having this belief that these people are tracking you?\n\nPatient: Well, let me think about the exact timeline... because I actually tried to map this out the other day when I was looking back through my Outlook calendar, trying to find the exact starting point of all this. If I really trace it back to the very first time I noticed the pattern, it’s been about two months now. Yeah, right around two months. \n\nI know this for a fact because it started right around the time I was putting together a rather complex estate transition plan for one of my older clients—a really lovely couple I've worked with since I first started my practice. I remember I had just finished a highly confidential meeting with them on a Tuesday afternoon, going over some very specific trust structures. And then that Thursday, I was at this gallery opening downtown. You know, one of those networking things you just have to show your face at in this business to keep up appearances. And the organizer of the event, who I barely even know, comes up to me and starts talking specifically about wealth transfer and legacy building, using the exact same highly specific phrasing I had just used behind closed doors in my private office two days prior. \n\nAt first, I tried to brush it off. I really did. I told myself, okay, maybe it's just an industry buzzword thing, right? A total coincidence. But then it just kept happening. The next week, a panel discussion I was invited to attend suddenly changed its topic to mirror a portfolio restructuring I was doing for a different client. And then the seating arrangements at the charity dinners started aligning perfectly with the prospects I was researching. \n\nSo if I'm looking at the whole picture, the realization that they are actively tracking my client meetings and sending me these signals... that's been going on for a solid two months. And honestly, these past eight weeks have felt like an absolute eternity, because when you're constantly on high alert, analyzing every single interaction, every email, every passing comment to see if it's a message from whoever is coordinating this... it just stretches time out. It takes over your whole mental calendar, you know? But yes, to answer your question, it's been about two months of this.\n\nDoctor: Has this belief about people tracking you been present continuously for at least one month?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, like I was just saying a minute ago, it’s been going on for about two months now. It’s not like they just track my client meetings on Mondays and Wednesdays and take the rest of the week off, you know? It doesn't stop just because the market closes. \n\nFor those entire two months—eight solid weeks, day in and day out—it has been a constant, everyday thing. I haven't had a single break from it. I wake up, and before I even check the overnight futures or look at my inbox, I’m already bracing myself for what signals they're going to send that day. Even on the weekends, when I'm just trying to decompress, maybe grab a coffee and review some prospect files at home, I’ll see or hear something that connects right back to a private conversation I had in my office on Thursday. \n\nThere hasn't been a single day in this whole period where I thought, 'Oh, okay, they've stopped paying attention to me.' It’s a continuous, unbroken line for the last two months of them monitoring who I'm meeting with and making sure I know about it. So, yes, very continuous. I haven't had a moment of peace from it since it started.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any other unusual beliefs or experiences besides people tracking you?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not really. Well, I mean, I'm still working. I haven't quit or been fired or anything like that. But... well, normally? I don't know if I'd say normally. It's definitely had an impact, which, honestly, is the most frustrating part of this whole ordeal.

It feels like walking into a trap. So I just decline the invitations now. I tell them I'm too busy with Q3 rebalancing or whatever excuse sounds plausible.

And it's not just the public stuff, either. It's affecting the day-to-day, which really bothers me because I pride myself on client service. But my practice has actually gotten a bit smaller recently. I’m just having trouble keeping up the same level of client contact I used to manage. It’s exhausting, you know? Every time I have a meeting, I have to be so hyper-aware of what I'm saying, wondering how it's going to be used against me later. It takes so much mental energy that by the time the meeting is over, I'm just drained. 

Because of that, I've missed some follow-ups. Nothing catastrophic, no one has lost money because I forgot to execute a trade, but... you know, the "soft" touches. The check-in calls to see how their kid's college tour went, or sending over a quick article I saw about municipal bonds that I thought they'd like. The kind of relationship-building stuff that keeps clients loyal. I just haven't had the bandwidth for it. I'm so focused on protecting the integrity of the information in the actual meetings that the follow-ups slip through the cracks. So, yes, I'm still functioning, I'm still managing portfolios, but the practice is definitely shrinking a bit because I just can't operate at the same volume or visibility that I used to before all this started happening.

Putting thoughts into my mind? Controlling them? No, absolutely not. That's... well, that's just as impossible as the broadcasting thing you asked about earlier, right? My mind is my own. Other beliefs? No, no, definitely not. I don't have any, you know, bizarre theories about aliens or the government or anything like that. It’s really just this one specific situation, which, honestly, is the whole reason I came in to see you in the first place. My mind is completely secure, it's just my environment that isn't.\n\nDoctor: Have you been able to keep working and handle your daily responsibilities pretty much normally, or has this belief caused a major drop in your functioning?\n\nPatient: Well, I mean, I'm still working. I haven't quit or been fired or anything like that. But... well, normally? I don't know if I'd say normally. It's definitely had an impact, which, honestly, is the most frustrating part of this whole ordeal. \n\nI used to be out there all the time, right? I was the guy who would go to every single chamber of commerce mixer, every charity golf tournament, every local business panel. I tell them I'm too busy with Q3 rebalancing or whatever excuse sounds plausible.\n\nAnd it's not just the public stuff, either. It's affecting the day-to-day, which really bothers me because I pride myself on client service. But my practice has actually gotten a bit smaller recently. I’m just having trouble keeping up the same level of client contact I used to manage. It’s exhausting, you know? Every time I have a meeting, I have to be so hyper-aware of what I'm saying, wondering how it's going to be used against me later. It takes so much mental energy that by the time the meeting is over, I'm just drained. \n\nBecause of that, I've missed some follow-ups. Nothing catastrophic, no one has lost money because I forgot to execute a trade, but... you know, the \"soft\" touches. The check-in calls to see how their kid's college tour went, or sending over a quick article I saw about municipal bonds that I thought they'd like. The kind of relationship-building stuff that keeps clients loyal. I just haven't had the bandwidth for it. I'm so focused on protecting the integrity of the information in the actual meetings that the follow-ups slip through the cracks. So, yes, I'm still functioning, I'm still managing portfolios, but the practice is definitely shrinking a bit because I just can't operate at the same volume or visibility that I used to before all this started happening.\n\nDoctor: Have you started, stopped, or changed any prescription medications, recreational drugs, or supplements around the time this began?\n\nPatient: No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I don't really take anything. I take a multivitamin in the morning, you know, just a standard one, nothing crazy, and maybe an ibuprofen if I have a headache from staring at spreadsheets too long, but that's it. I haven't started any new prescriptions, haven't stopped any... I don't even have a primary care doctor I see regularly enough to get prescriptions, to be honest. I'm generally pretty healthy. \n\nAnd as for recreational drugs, absolutely not. I mean, in my line of work, you have to be sharp. My routine is exactly the same as it's always been. I wake up, have my coffee—just black, no sugar, maybe two cups max—take my vitamin, and get to work. That's it. It doesn't just pop into my head from some outside force. I mean, can you imagine the liability issues if someone else was controlling my recommendations? The SEC would have a field day with that. \n\nBut no, seriously, my thoughts are 100% mine. I generate them, I process them, I act on them. The problem, like I keep trying to explain, isn't what's happening inside my head. The inside of my head is perfectly fine, perfectly secure, perfectly logical. The problem is what happens after the thoughts leave my head. It's when I take those perfectly normal, independently generated thoughts and speak them out loud in a confidential meeting. I just can't. The timing is always too perfect, too deliberate. \n\nSo, no, there's absolutely nothing else outside of that. It's taking up so much of my mental energy just trying to navigate this one issue, there really wouldn't even be room in my head for anything else anyway.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any periods lasting two weeks or longer when you felt depressed, down, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy?\n\nPatient: Depressed? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I know I just spent all that time telling you about how I'm skipping my Thursday night basketball games and blowing off those jazz nights downtown, and I realize that probably sounds exactly like someone who is depressed, but it really isn't that. I'm not sad. I don't have this... this dark cloud hanging over me, or feelings of hopelessness, or anything like you see in the commercials. I don't sit around crying or feeling miserable about my life.\n\nI mean, I know what depression looks like. In my line of work, you see it firsthand. When the market takes a massive hit—like back during the initial COVID crash, or even some of the tech sector corrections we've seen recently—I've had clients call me up, literally in tears, completely despondent because they think their retirement is ruined. They get so down they can barely function, completely consumed by the sadness and the panic of it all. That is not what I’m experiencing. My mood itself is actually pretty stable. I don't wake up feeling miserable. When I go for my 5:30 AM jog, I'm not dragging myself out of bed feeling like life is pointless. \n\nIt's exactly like I was saying before, it's just an energy thing. The mental bandwidth it takes to deal with the people in the arts and finance circles who are monitoring my client meetings—that's what exhausts me. It takes so much focus to constantly analyze the signals they're sending, the panel topics, the seating arrangements at these charity dinners. By the time I'm done with the workday, I just don't have the fuel left in the tank to go socialize or make small talk. But it's a lack of fuel, not a surplus of sadness. It’s just a flat, empty tank. If you took all that tracking stuff away, I'd be perfectly fine, I’m sure of it. So, no, to answer your question, I haven't had any two-week stretches of feeling depressed or down. I'm just trying to navigate a very complicated, very exhausting situation without completely running myself into the ground.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever heard voices or seen things that seemed completely real to you, even when no one else could?\n\nPatient: Voices? No, no. Definitely not. I want to be really clear about that, because I know when I explain the whole... the situation with the arts and finance circles, it probably sounds like something out of a movie, and people might assume I'm sitting in a dark room hearing whispers or something. But that is absolutely not what is happening. I don't hear anything that isn't actually there. \n\nWhen I'm in my office on the 14th floor, looking over a client's 401k allocations or drafting a quarterly report, it is completely quiet. I mean, I hear the HVAC system—we have this terrible vent right above my desk that rattles constantly, which is annoying on its own—and I hear the traffic down on the street, but I'm not hearing disembodied voices or people talking to me when the room is empty. My hearing is perfectly normal. If anything, I just pay closer attention to the real conversations happening around me now, but there are no imaginary voices. Nothing like that. \n\nAnd I don't see things, either. Like, no visions or mirages or whatever. Everything I see is one hundred percent physically real. When I see someone from the local arts council sitting two tables away from me at a restaurant, they are a real flesh-and-blood person eating a real meal. When an invitation shows up on my desk, it's actual heavy-stock paper. When that panel topic gets announced right after my meeting, it's a real email sitting right there in my actual inbox. I could print it out and hand it to you, you know? I'm not conjuring things out of thin air. It’s just that the real things, the real people in this city, are the ones coordinating this whole tracking thing. So, no. No voices, no seeing things. Just the actual, physical reality of what they're doing."
